#2115. West Ham Show Their Worst And Best In Extraordinary Cardiff Draw

West Ham’s extraordinary 3-3 draw against Cardiff City was quite possibly the most bizarre game I’ve watched this season. At half-time, with Scott Parker’s new team trailing by three goals, I genuinely wondered whether we were about to concede six or seven. We hadn’t just been beaten in that opening 45 minutes; we’d completely capitulated.

Yet somehow, the same group of players emerged for the second half and produced a performance almost unrecognisable from what had gone before. West Ham dominated Cardiff, scored three goals and could quite easily have won the game. Jarrod Bowen, who had been largely anonymous before the break, suddenly looked like the best player on the pitch by an absolute mile.

I would love to know what Scott Parker said at half-time, because whatever happened in that dressing room had an extraordinary effect. This was a manager who hadn’t even taken a training session with his new players, yet the transformation was incredible. Whether it was his words, the substitutions or simply the players finding something within themselves, I haven’t seen a turnaround quite like it for a long time.

The frustrating thing was that West Ham actually started reasonably well. There was some intensity, some urgency and a willingness to compete for second balls that had been conspicuously absent during the final weeks of Nuno Espírito Santo’s reign.

Parker’s first team selection included Soungoutou Magassa as a specialist defensive midfielder, while Divine Mukasa was given the freedom to play further forward. Both decisions made sense to me, particularly after watching Mukasa spend so much time trying to compensate for problems elsewhere in midfield under Nuno.

Morato was winning tackles, Mukasa looked comfortable on the ball and West Ham appeared to be playing with a little more purpose. Unfortunately, it didn’t last.

After 11 minutes, Joel Moylan was afforded far too much space outside the penalty area and unleashed an absolute thunderbolt into the top corner. There may have been a slight deflection off Max Kilman, but the bigger concern was the amount of room Cardiff had been allowed in central areas.

Even then, West Ham weren’t completely out of the contest. However, the confidence began draining out of the players, and what followed was a collapse that reminded me of everything we’ve been watching for far too long.

In the 37th minute, a simple long ball over the top exposed Morato’s lack of pace at left-back. He couldn’t recover, conceded a penalty and Moylan duly converted to double Cardiff’s advantage.

Two minutes later, it was 3-0. An inswinging corner was met by Moylan at the near post, with Jarrod Bowen somehow finding himself responsible for challenging him in the air. Moylan completed his hat-trick, and West Ham’s defending was absolutely dreadful.

Three goals conceded in three completely different ways: a long-range shot, a straightforward ball over the top and a corner. It was almost as though Cardiff were being invited to choose how they wanted to score next.

What concerned me most wasn’t simply the defending. It was the complete disappearance of confidence.

West Ham looked shell-shocked. Players who had started the match with some urgency suddenly appeared frightened of making mistakes. There was no cohesion, no understanding and precious little belief.

I genuinely feared the worst. Having watched the dreadful defeat against West Bromwich Albion just days earlier, this felt like another team completely falling apart.

There appears to be some serious footballing PTSD within this group after years of being crap. The moment something goes wrong, the confidence seems to disappear, and one setback quickly becomes two or three.

At half-time, I wasn’t wondering how West Ham could get back into the match. I was wondering how many more Cardiff might score.

Parker made three substitutions at the interval, introducing Ezra Mayers, Mohamadou Kanté and Joël Piroe in place of Morato, Magassa and Taty Castellanos.

They were bold changes, but they were absolutely necessary. West Ham needed more pace, more energy and a completely different approach to the game.

Mukasa scored West Ham’s first goal in a remarkable comeback

Suddenly, West Ham were pressing Cardiff, winning possession and moving the ball forward with purpose. There was an intensity to their play that simply hadn’t existed during the closing stages of the first half.

Joël Veltman began getting forward down the right, combining with Bowen and providing genuine attacking width. Kanté brought tremendous energy to midfield, carrying the ball forward and running directly at Cardiff’s defence.

Even Joël Piroe, despite a couple of poor early touches, was at least dropping deeper and attempting to become involved in the game.

West Ham were playing much more directly, regularly looking for balls behind Cardiff’s defence rather than simply passing possession around without any real threat. It wasn’t always pretty, and at times it was almost route-one football, but it was causing Cardiff enormous problems.

The home side had looked completely comfortable before half-time. Now they were struggling to cope with the speed and aggression of West Ham’s attacking play.

I don’t know precisely what Parker said to the players during the interval, but I’d have loved to have been a fly on the wall.

Of course, the tactical changes made a difference, but this was about more than tactics. The players suddenly looked as though they believed they could compete again.

The comeback began in the 57th minute with a genuinely lovely goal from Divine Mukasa.

Bowen produced a beautifully weighted chipped pass over the Cardiff defence, and Mukasa timed his run perfectly. His control with his right foot was exquisite before he delicately lifted the ball over Nathan Trott with his left.

It was a wonderful piece of football and exactly the sort of attacking quality we’ve been crying out for.

More importantly, it gave West Ham something to believe in.

The Hammers continued pushing forward, with Bowen becoming increasingly influential and Veltman offering support down the right. Cardiff were beginning to look uncomfortable, particularly when West Ham played early balls into the space behind their defensive line.

In the 65th minute, another direct ball from Bowen was cleverly flicked on by Piroe. Arne Engels timed his run beautifully and finished past Trott to make it 3-2.

From looking completely dead and buried, West Ham were suddenly within one goal of an equaliser.

Kanté produced an excellent opportunity after Mavropanos picked him out with a lovely pass. His first touch was superb, but Trott made a brilliant save to deny him.

Cardiff were retreating deeper and deeper, desperately trying to protect their lead. West Ham, meanwhile, were playing with a confidence and attacking intent that had been completely absent just half an hour earlier.

It was extraordinary to watch the transformation in our captain. In the first half, he had looked just as nervous and uncertain as everyone else. After the break, almost everything good West Ham produced seemed to involve him.

He was drifting into central areas, creating opportunities, playing clever passes and generally dictating proceedings.

In the 81st minute, West Ham finally got the equaliser their second-half performance deserved.

A corner initially appeared to have come to nothing, but Bowen kept the attack alive and swung another dangerous ball into the penalty area. Max Kilman was still forward and produced a superb half-volley to beat Trott.

I could scarcely believe what I was watching.

The remarkable thing was that West Ham weren’t satisfied with rescuing a point. They continued attacking and looked the more likely side to score a winner.

Edvin Austbø, who had replaced Manor Solomon, brought an immediate willingness to run at defenders. In the 89th minute, he unleashed a powerful shot that Trott could only parry back into his penalty area.

There was a real whiff of panic about Cardiff by this stage. Having been three goals ahead at half-time, they now looked desperate for the final whistle.

A minute later, Bowen produced another wonderful piece of jiggery-pokery before chipping the ball towards the far post. Ezra Mayers made an excellent run into the penalty area and attempted a left-footed volley that went tantalisingly close.

Even in stoppage time, West Ham were still creating opportunities.

In the 92nd minute, Bowen delivered yet another dangerous inswinging ball, this time finding Tomáš Souček. The midfielder directed his header on target, only for Trott to produce an excellent save.

It would have been an extraordinary winner, but even without a fourth goal, West Ham had completed a comeback that looked utterly impossible at half-time.

I suspect Cardiff were extremely grateful there weren’t another ten minutes left to play.

#2114. Newcastle United owners full commitment with now £900m investment in club

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The Newcastle United owners bought the club from Mike Ashley 61 months ago.

The 7 October 2021 seeing Mike Ashley become, at last, the former owner of the club after 14+ ambition-free years, where he had simply done everything he could to enrich himself and his retail empire, at the expense of the football club.

The new/current Newcastle United owners paid £305m to own the club over five years ago.

However, subsequent cash injections have been put in.

The latest has now been made public by Companies House on 4 November 2026.

The Newcastle United owners putting a new major cash injection of £95m into the football club, this takes the overall investment in the club to now over £900Million.

Any further investment in the club is always revealed via Companies House first, before they (the Newcastle United owners) formally declare it themselves in a statement. The Newcastle United owners are duty bound legally to file the info with Companies House.

One new share allotted with the stated purpose of only to allow the £95m cash injection to be put into the club. The Companies House update shows that this latest investment happened on 19 October 2026 and it always takes a couple of weeks or so once Companies House receive the filing, for that update to be available for the public to see.

This was the case with each of the previous further investment amounts put into the club, since the original takeover in October 2021, as detailed below.

The breakdown of where this £904m+ figure comes from:

7 October 2021 – £305m – This is the money the new/current Newcastle United owners paid to Mike Ashley.

9 November 2021 – £38.5m – Additional amount of money invested into the club by the Newcastle United owners.

24 January 2022 – £40.0m – Additional money invested into the club by Newcastle United owners.

26 October 2022 – £70.4m – Additional money invested into club by Newcastle United owners.

10 February 2023 – £57.0m – Additional money invested into the club by Newcastle United owners

22 August 2023 – £60.0m – Additional money invested into the club by the Newcastle United owners

28 March 2024 – £37.0m – Additional money invested into the club by the Newcastle United owners

30 October 2024 – £35.0m – Additional amount of money invested into the club by the Newcastle United owners

31 December 2024 – £15.0m – Additional amount of money invested into the club by the Newcastle United owners

8 September 2025 – £106.5m – Additional amount of money invested into the club by the Newcastle United owners

9 December 2025 – £45.0m – This additional amount of money invested into the club by the Newcastle United owners

19 October 2026 – £95.0m – This additional amount of money invested into the club by the Newcastle United owners

These twelve figures above, totalling £904.4m.

So £305m originally paid to Mike Ashley, then the new/current Newcastle United owners now having committed another £599.4m into their investment / football club.

Newcastle United still playing catch up and this extra £95.0m put into the club, used for day to day running costs and of course in general terms, towards investment in new signings, plus potentially training ground and new stadium…

So the Newcastle United owners heading swiftly to a point whereby they will have committed £1billion worth of investment to their asset, their football club.

#2113. Scott Parker Moves Quickly To Fix West Ham Coaching Concern

West Ham United have confirmed that Jonathan Hill has joined Scott Parker’s backroom team as assistant coach, bringing additional experience to the Hammers’ new management setup. Hill has previously worked alongside Parker at several clubs and arrives with a strong background in football analysis.

The appointment was announced on West Ham’s official website, with Hill joining Mark Noble, Steve Potts, Gerard Prenderville and Billy Lepine on the coaching staff.

It was only after West Ham’s remarkable 3-3 draw against Cardiff City in Parker’s first match as Hammers boss that I discovered he’d added another member to his backroom team. And I have to say, I’m absolutely delighted.

I think having Mark Noble in the dugout is incredible. His passion for West Ham, understanding of the club and ability to connect with players should bring something invaluable to the dressing room.

But the one concern I had about Noble’s appointment was his lack of extensive first-team coaching experience.

That isn’t a criticism of Noble, far from it. I just felt Parker needed somebody alongside him with a strong background in coaching and tactical analysis.

By bringing in Jonathan Hill, he has immediately addressed what I considered a glaring gap in the backroom team.

Hill’s previous working relationship with Parker should also be an advantage. There is already an understanding between the two, rather than the new head coach having to build that relationship from scratch.

And nobody who witnessed the first half against Cardiff can be in any doubt that this West Ham squad will benefit from all the additional coaching and tactical expertise it can get.

The players clearly have ability, as the comeback demonstrated, but there is still an enormous amount of work to do.

For me, this is an encouraging appointment. Parker has retained the West Ham connections and passion that Noble and Potts provide, while adding another experienced football man to help with the coaching.

It’s early days, of course, but I’m pleased to see the new manager strengthening his staff so quickly.

#2112. Oxford City vs Leicester City - prediction, team news, lineups

By Matt Law | 04 Nov 2026 16:25, Last updated: 04 Nov 2026 22:11

Fallen giants Leicester City will be aiming to avoid what would be one of the biggest shocks in recent FA Cup history when they head to National League North outfit Oxford City on Friday night in the first round of the tournament.

It is the first time that Leicester have competed in this round since 2008, and Oxford City have been given the chance to claim a huge scalp in the tournament.

Oxford City have managed to progress to the second round of the FA Cup on three previous occasions - 1969-70, 2017-18 and 2020-21, so the club have previous when it comes to advancing past this stage of the famous cup competition.

The Hoops will enter this match off the back of a disappointing result, though, going down 3-1 at home to South Shields in the National League North on Saturday.

Ross Jenkins' side are currently second in the National League North, picking up 27 points from their opening 14 matches of the campaign, two points behind South Shields following the clash between the top two.

Oxford City have had to win three matches to reach this stage of the FA Cup, overcoming Dorchester, Enfield Town and Torquay to be present in the first round.

Leicester, meanwhile, will enter this match off the back of a 2-2 draw with Stevenage, with the result leaving them in 10th spot in the League One table.

The Foxes have won three of their last five league games, but there is no getting away from the fact that it has been a disappointing start to the season as a whole.

Leicester famously won this competition back in 2021, recording a 1-0 victory over Chelsea courtesy of a second-half effort from Youri Tielemans.

Russell Martin is still under pressure at Leicester but remains at the helm, with the 40-year-old bidding to help the Foxes secure a return to the Championship.

Leicester's last FA Cup fixture brought a 2-1 defeat to Southampton in the last-16 stage of the 2025-26 competition.

Oxford City will be looking to Tyrone Marsh for goals on Friday, with the 32-year-old netting nine times in all competitions at the start of the 2026-27 campaign.

There will also be a position in the team for Scott Pollock, who has been another key performer this season, coming up with six goals and two assists in 13 appearances.

Ludwig Francillette and Josh Ashby are also set to be notable starters.

As for Leicester, there are set to be a number of changes to the team that took to the field for the 2-2 draw with Stevenage in the league last time out.

However, Ben Nelson and Jakub Stolarczyk are both out of the match through injury.

Conor Chaplin should be introduced in the final third of the field, while 19-year-old Ilari Kangasniemi is expected to be a notable starter at the back.

Fellow teenager Louis Page is expected to be among those to be rested.

#2111. “Forceful and Aggressive” Parker’s Passion Already Making A Mark At West Ham

West Ham manager Scott Parker’s comments following last night’s incredible comeback against Cardiff City were an absolute joy to listen to. Having watched the Hammers recover from three goals down to draw 3-3, I was already feeling considerably more optimistic about our prospects. But listening to Parker afterwards was almost as encouraging as the second-half performance itself.

In the modern game, much is made of tactics, and rightly so. But one thing I believe gets underplayed is not only man-management, but a head coach’s personality. And quite frankly, Parker has bundles of it.

I have to say, it’s a refreshing change from what we’ve seen in recent seasons. Nuno Espírito Santo was a softly spoken man, not prone to using a few words when considerably more would do, and the less said about Graham Potter as a leader and orator, the better at this point. But my word, it’s thrilling to hear Parker speak.

Speaking in his post-match interview with West Ham’s official website, Parker described the transformation in his team after the break:

“It was a forceful team, an aggressive team, a front-footed team, which was obviously a big improvement.”

That’s exactly what I want to hear from a West Ham manager, and more importantly, it’s exactly what I want to see from a West Ham team.

As Martins morning round-up demonstrated, the difference between the two halves was extraordinary.

We went from a team seemingly incapable of stringing together a meaningful attack to one that looked determined to take the game to the opposition.

And Parker clearly recognised the difference.

He was particularly critical of the backwards passing and the lack of purpose in possession during the opening 45 minutes.

Then came another observation that I found particularly encouraging:

“There’s no point in just building, building, building.”

Again, music to my ears and we saw that with the first two goals from Mukasa and Engels.

For far too long, we’ve watched West Ham move the ball around without appearing particularly interested in doing anything with it.

Parker wants players taking risks, making forward runs, delivering crosses and getting bodies into the penalty area.

That doesn’t guarantee success, of course, but it’s a pretty good place to start.

What really impressed me, though, wasn’t simply Parker’s analysis of the football.

It cannot be overstated quite how much good it does the fanbase to see a manager walking over to applaud the travelling supporters, becoming one with them, and then speaking so passionately about what he wants to achieve.

There were 3,200 West Ham fans at Cardiff, and after the dreadful opening 45 minutes, they deserved something to cheer.

And I’ll tell you this much: if Parker communicates with supporters like this, one can only imagine how effective he might be when speaking to his players.

Of course, being a good speaker doesn’t automatically make somebody a good manager.

But I’ve always believed that one of the most immediate improvements West Ham needed was motivation.

We have talented players. I’ve said that repeatedly. What we’ve lacked is somebody capable of getting them playing with urgency, belief and a bit of fire in their bellies.

Parker certainly sounds like somebody who understands that.

I was also absolutely delighted to hear him say how eager he was to get the players together and start asking questions.

He admitted that he couldn’t fully understand how the performance had changed so dramatically between the two halves.

And rather than simply celebrating the comeback, he was already thinking about what needed to improve before Saturday’s trip to Blackburn Rovers.

It’s also worth remembering that Parker had only met the players at the airport that morning, having been confirmed as West Ham’s new head coach just hours before kick-off.

He has barely had an opportunity to work with them.

Judging his tactics, selections and long-term suitability can come later. There will be plenty of time for that.

But I’ve always thought there was one obvious and immediate improvement that could be made to this West Ham team, and that was getting the players motivated.

After listening to Parker, I have considerably fewer worries on that score.

I genuinely cannot wait for the next game.

#2107. Mark Noble’s Return To West Ham Dugout Comes With A Catch

The sight of Mark Noble sitting alongside Scott Parker in last night’s game has prompted plenty of debate among West Ham supporters.

For many, the question is simple. If Noble does not hold the UEFA coaching qualifications, how can he be part of the first-team setup and occupy a place on the bench?

The issue has become a hot topic among supporters, particularly as UEFA regulations require coaches working at various levels of the professional game to hold the appropriate licences or be actively working towards them. UEFA’s coaching pathway runs from C Licence through to Pro Licence, with increasing levels of qualification required for senior positions.

However, the reality is that not everyone seated in a technical area is necessarily registered as a coach.

Modern football clubs employ a wide variety of football staff whose responsibilities can overlap with the first team without them formally holding coaching positions. Player liaison officers, football advisers, technical assistants, performance specialists and football operations staff can all be involved on matchdays without being registered as coaches.

That distinction could prove crucial in understanding Noble’s position.

He brings invaluable experience and knowledge to the team. Few individuals understand the pressures and expectations of representing West Ham better than the club’s former captain. His influence around a dressing room, particularly during periods of transition, could be viewed as every bit as important as the contribution of a traditional coach.

Nevertheless, the situation raises an understandable question among fans. Yet as his role continues to evolve, supporters will remain curious about the precise nature of his responsibilities and whether formal coaching qualifications may eventually become part of his longer-term pathway in football.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

Squad Mentor and Sporting Director. Next, move on.

I’m not concerned with his involvement as part of Scotty’s team, as long as he isn’t sacked with the manager and team when the time comes (as it inevitably always does eventually)

Thanks Morty, you hit the nail on the head.

I am curious with excitement and encouragement.

Finally, attention turns to the upcoming trip to Fulham and whether Newcastle can find a much-needed response.

It’s a frustrated, occasionally heated and typically humorous Mag Pod, with three supporters trying to make sense of a season that’s heading in the wrong direction.

#2105. West Ham Owners’ ‘Marriage Of Convenience’ Could End With Staveley Takeover

West Ham’s ownership saga has taken another interesting turn following comments from former football executive Christian Purslow, who believes Daniel Křetínský and David Sullivan could eventually sell the club to Amanda Staveley once the Hammers return to the Premier League.

Speaking to football journalist Henry Winter on The Football Boardroom podcast, Purslow described the relationship between West Ham’s two principal shareholders as a “marriage of convenience” and questioned why the previously announced agreement to purchase Vanessa Gold’s shares has still not been formally completed.

Regular readers of Claret & Hugh, and indeed viewers of Hammers Chat, will not be particularly surprised by any of this. I’ve been describing Sullivan and Křetínský as business partners for some time, and the possibility of Staveley eventually returning to the negotiating table is something we’ve discussed at length.

Purslow’s comments came during a fascinating discussion with Henry Winter about West Ham’s ownership situation, prompted by the dismissal of Nuno Espírito Santo and the appointment of Scott Parker.

The former Liverpool and Aston Villa chief executive suggested that Sullivan and Křetínský may have very little in common, but they share one overriding ambition: getting West Ham back into the Premier League as quickly as possible.

That, according to Purslow, is enough to keep their working relationship together, even if their longer-term ambitions for the football club are different.

And frankly, I think he’s absolutely right.

Ever since the agreement was reached for Křetínský to purchase the bulk of Vanessa Gold’s shares, with Sullivan increasing his own holding from approximately 38.8% to 40%, I’ve referred to the pair as business partners. Indeed, Claret & Hugh reported last month that a club insider had specifically described their relationship as a “joint partnership”.

I appreciate that this might be uncomfortable for some West Ham supporters to hear, particularly those who hoped Sullivan’s departure from his executive position would signal the beginning of the end of his involvement.

But let’s be fair, a man who wants less financial involvement in a football club doesn’t ordinarily increase his shareholding. Whatever anybody thinks of Sullivan, the proposed arrangement would leave him owning approximately 40% of West Ham, and that’s hardly the behaviour of somebody desperate to walk away immediately.

Staveley has been locked out of West Ham for now

What I found particularly interesting was Purslow questioning something we’ve also discussed repeatedly on this website. Why has the agreement to increase Křetínský’s shareholding to 46% still not been formally completed?

The arrangement was announced back in September, with the existing shareholders exercising their rights to purchase Vanessa Gold’s stake and subsequently agreeing to redistribute shares. As our original investigation into the transaction explained, the process was designed to leave Křetínský as West Ham’s largest shareholder, Sullivan on approximately 40% and Tripp Smith on around 11%.

Yet here we are in November, and the anticipated confirmation of the completed transaction has still not arrived. Purslow admitted he found that puzzling and wondered whether the agreement might have encountered difficulties, although he was careful to acknowledge that he did not know whether that was the case.

I completely agree with him that the delay is odd, although I wouldn’t go so far as to suggest the agreement has collapsed. In fact, when Claret & Hugh last enquired, we were assured that there were no problems with the transaction and that completion was expected soon.

Nevertheless, there is another important point here. Křetínský indicated that he would engage with supporters once his increased shareholding had been finalised, and we’re still waiting for that conversation.

Given the importance of the proposed ownership changes, I don’t think it’s unreasonable for supporters to expect some clarity about when the transaction will be completed and what the future structure of the club will look like.

Kretinsky successfully blocked Vanessa Gold’s attempts to sell her shareholding to Staveley but has yet to purchase her shares according to Purslow

Perhaps the most fascinating part of Purslow’s analysis concerned Amanda Staveley, who previously attempted to purchase the Gold family’s stake before the existing shareholders moved to prevent her from acquiring it.

Purslow suggested that once West Ham have secured promotion to the Premier League, both Sullivan and Křetínský could decide that the time is right to sell the entire football club. He also identified Staveley as a possible buyer, pointing to her previous interest, the work she has already undertaken examining the club and her ambitions for the London Stadium.

His assessment was particularly interesting:

“I have a feeling Amanda Staveley might well reappear because she would be the natural buyer for the whole club.”

Now, this is obviously Purslow’s prediction rather than confirmation of any agreement between the shareholders and Staveley. But I have to say, it’s a scenario I’ve considered entirely plausible for some time.

I’ve never fully believed that Staveley had gone away completely. For somebody who appeared so determined to purchase a football club, there has been remarkably little public indication of her pursuing another opportunity since her attempt to buy into West Ham was blocked.

Of course, that doesn’t mean she hasn’t been exploring other possibilities privately. But we already know she has shown a serious interest in West Ham, and Claret & Hugh previously revealed that discussions had taken place over the possibility of her acquiring Sullivan’s shares if the Gold family route proved unsuccessful.

Purslow also raised the question of valuations. He suggested Staveley’s previous proposal valued West Ham at around £600million, while Sullivan has historically placed a considerably higher value on the club. Promotion would clearly change the financial picture, making a potential sale more attractive than it would be while West Ham remain in the Championship.

The suggestion that Sullivan and Křetínský are effectively working together until West Ham secure promotion makes a certain amount of sense to me. Both have an enormous financial interest in the club returning to the Premier League, and that shared objective could be enough to maintain their partnership regardless of any differences between them.

It also puts the appointment of Scott Parker into an interesting context. Having backed Nuno to lead the promotion campaign during the summer, the shareholders have now agreed to change direction and appoint a manager with three Championship promotions on his CV.

Purslow clearly believes promotion could become the catalyst for something much bigger than another managerial change. His suggestion is that the two principal shareholders might eventually decide to cash in, potentially creating the opportunity for Staveley to return with a proposal to purchase the whole club rather than simply a minority stake.

Whether that happens remains to be seen, and there is certainly no evidence of an agreed sale. But I find it difficult to dismiss the possibility, particularly given everything we’ve already been told about the relationship between Sullivan and Křetínský and Staveley’s previous determination to get involved.

For me, the most revealing aspect of Purslow’s comments is that he has independently arrived at a number of the same questions we’ve been asking for months. Why is the share transaction taking so long? What exactly is the relationship between Sullivan and Křetínský? And has Amanda Staveley really disappeared from the picture?

I suspect we haven’t heard the last of any of those three questions.

#2104. Gaziantep vs Kasimpasa - prediction, team news, lineups

By Joshua Cole | 04 Nov 2026 16:42, Last updated: 04 Nov 2026 16:42

Gaziantep will be desperate to halt their alarming slide when they welcome Kasimpasa to Gaziantep Stadyumu on Friday in the Turkish Super Lig.

The hosts have lost five consecutive league matches and are hovering just above the relegation zone with eight points from their opening 10 fixtures, while their visitors occupy fifth place with 17 points and arrive unbeaten in their last three league outings.

Gaziantep have endured a miserable spell in the league, with their latest setback coming in a 2-0 defeat away to Trabzonspor.

Orhan Ak's side struggled to make an impact against the Black Sea outfit, conceding once in each half as they suffered another damaging result following defeats against Erzurumspor, Istanbul Basaksehir, Corum and Kocaelispor.

Their 4-0 Turkish Cup victory over Etimesgutspor provided some relief, but that result has done little to disguise their domestic difficulties, particularly as they have scored just twice across their last five league matches while conceding 12 goals.

The lack of attacking output is becoming a significant concern for Ak, whose team have struggled to turn possession into meaningful opportunities and have repeatedly found themselves chasing matches after falling behind.

Gaziantep have also struggled to establish Gaziantep Stadyumu as a source of points, failing to win any game as hosts yet, drawing two and losing three times in five home matches.

However, the Falcons are unbeaten in their last five meetings with the Apaches, picking up three wins and two draws, while they have also avoided defeat in their last three encounters against them as hosts, winning twice and drawing once.

Kasimpasa, meanwhile, have enjoyed a considerably more encouraging opening to the campaign, losing just one of their 10 league games so far while recording four wins and five draws.

Emre Belozoglu's team were held to an entertaining 2-2 draw by Besiktas in their previous league outing, with Claudio Winck and Michael Rafferty finding the net as they twice threatened to take all three points.

That result extended their unbeaten league sequence to three matches, following victories over Eyupspor and Samsunspor, while they also recorded a 3-1 win over Corluspor in the Turkish Cup, extending their unbeaten run across all competitions to four matches.

Kasimpasa have also collected useful points on their travels this season, recording 10 points from five away games, with three wins, one draw and one defeat, which should give them optimism ahead of this trip.

Gaziantep have several availability concerns ahead of Friday's encounter, with Myenty Abena facing suspension following a yellow-card accumulation, while Ulrich Meleke, Ogun Ozcicek, Arda Kizildag and Sontje Hansen are among those carrying injuries.

Serdar Dursun is also expected to miss out, while Nazim Sangare and Fuat Bavuk remain unavailable.

Kasimpasa have fewer confirmed concerns, although Kamil Ahmet Corekci is expected to remain sidelined with an Achilles tendon injury.

Godfried Frimpong and Kevin Mouanga are also carrying fitness problems, leaving the visitors potentially short of defensive options, while no further suspensions have been reported.

Adrian Benedyczak has scored six goals in the league this season, and he will be the man to watch for the Apaches in this encounter.

Dadakdeniz; Perez, Abena, Sylla, Calhanoglu; Bacuna; Sorescu, Gidado, Maxim, Kozlowski; Stewart

Gianniotis; Jensen, Ilie, Arous, Winck; Demirbay, Mendes; Hajradinovic, Rak-Sakyi, Kol; Benedyczak

Gaziantep's home advantage and historical record in this fixture could make Friday's encounter more competitive than the league standings suggest, but their current defensive problems are difficult to overlook.

Kasimpasa have shown considerably more attacking consistency, and their recent form should ultimately see them claim all three points.

#2103. Jurgen Klopp delivers devastating news to Nick Woltemade

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Nick Woltemade not hearing what he wanted to from Jurgen Klopp.

A 24-man Germany squad named on Thursday and Malick Thiaw included.

However, no Nick Woltemade making the cut.

The last international break lasted three weeks and four matches, Jurgen Klopp called up 44 players in total.

Needing to name 20 less than that figure, the Germany boss omitting the Newcastle United striker currently on loan with Juventus.

Jurgen Klopp after naming his Germany squad for the November internationals: “After having a 44-man roster in September, it was difficult to make these choices, though in a positive sense, that is actually good news, as more players deserved to be included…The more quality you have at your disposal, the more challenging, in a good way, it is to make the decisions you have to make.”

Nick Woltemade wasn’t alone in getting the devastating news, as Karim Adeyemi, Nadiem Amiri and David Raum were among the others left out of the squad.

When you check out the reality of the situation though, maybe it shouldn’t have been a shock.

Nick Woltemade has had very limited opportunities with Juventus in Serie A. Only cameos off the bench until starting two of their last three league games. Big Nick with no goals in Serie A yet but he has scored in all three of Juventus’ Europa League matches this season.

Big Nick has lost out to Niclas Fuellkrug when Jurgen Klopp named this squad.

The 33-year-old returned to Werder Bremen in the summer after a shocking time at West Ham, Fuellkrug has scored 12 goals in 10 appearances in all competitions this season.

Jurgen Klopp commenting on the veteran striker: “He played quite a few games and he has absolutely been performing. He has scored all types of goals and has had an unbelievable influence on Werder Bremen, not only through his goals but the way in which he has played. It was a pretty easy nomination to make and it was a pleasure to let him know he was in.”

Germany face Serbia in Belgrade on November 13 and host the Netherlands in Berlin three days later.

Goalkeepers: Jonas Urbig, Marc-Andre ter Stegen, Alexander Nübel

Defence: Waldemar Anton, Nathaniel Brown, Finn Jeltsch, Maximilian Mittelstädt, Nico Schlotterbeck, Jonathan Tah, Malick Thiaw, Philipp Treu

Midfield: Tom Bischof, Said El Mala, Bajan Gruda, Lennart Karl, Joshua Kimmich, Wael Mohya, Felix Nmecha, Aleksandar Pavlovic, Derry Scherhant, Florian Wirtz

Strikers: Younes Ebnoutalib, Niclas Füllkrug, Kai Havertz

Interesting to see that Jurgen Klopp kept faith with Malick Thiaw despite the United defender getting dropped by Matthias Jaissle for recent Newcastle matches.

#2102. “Incredible Performance” Scott Parker May Have Unlocked A New Jarrod Bowen At West Ham

Whilst West Ham may have stunk the place out in the first half against Cardiff City last night, there was an awful lot to be excited about in the second. And none more so than Jarrod Bowen, who produced an absolutely magnificent performance as the Hammers fought back from three goals down to rescue a 3-3 draw.

The Irons captain was imperious, dominant and displayed the sort of leadership that I personally don’t think we’ve seen from him before. This wasn’t simply a case of our best player producing a few moments of individual brilliance. Bowen appeared to take responsibility for dragging the entire team back into the contest.

And don’t just take my word for it. West Ham right-back Joël Veltman described how Bowen had given his teammates something of a telling-off as the starting eleven sat down to lick their wounds at half-time, three-nil down. “Our captain stepped up when we needed him,” said the Dutchman, and he clearly wasn’t wrong.

Bowen’s second-half performance was extraordinary. Starting on the right but drifting inside towards the middle of the pitch, often popping up in a number ten position, the captain created absolute havoc. Cardiff simply couldn’t handle him.

Whether he had been given greater freedom by new West Ham boss Scott Parker or was simply taking the initiative himself, Bowen suddenly looked like a player who had been released from his shackles. He had a hand in all three West Ham goals, demonstrating just how much damage he can do when he’s allowed to influence the game from different areas of the pitch.

First came the beautifully weighted pass that allowed Divine Mukasa to produce a wonderful chipped finish. Then another Bowen pass was cleverly flicked on by Joël Piroe, allowing Arne Engels to race through and score his first West Ham goal. Finally, with eight minutes remaining, Bowen delivered the dangerous cross that Maximilian Kilman converted to complete the comeback.

It was the sort of performance that screamed, I am the best player in this division. And frankly, I think he is. He could even have finished with more assists, creating late opportunities for Ezra Mayers and Tomáš Souček as West Ham pushed for an unlikely winner.

Parker will have been delighted with Bowen’s incredible performance

Neither Julen Lopetegui, Graham Potter nor Nuno Espírito Santo consistently managed to get the very best out of Jarrod Bowen. That’s not to suggest he hasn’t performed brilliantly under those managers, because he quite clearly has. But too often we’ve seen him isolated on the right, expected to create something from nothing while the rest of the team struggled to get forward.

Against Cardiff, particularly in the second half, things looked rather different. Bowen was finding space centrally, combining with teammates and getting into positions where he could genuinely hurt the opposition. It’s early days, of course, and Parker has barely had an opportunity to work with the squad, but perhaps the new manager will recognise that one of the easiest ways to improve West Ham is simply to get our best player into the most threatening positions.

It doesn’t have to be particularly complicated. Give Bowen the freedom to influence games and let the opposition worry about stopping him, rather than asking him to spend much of the match chasing possession in areas where he can’t do any damage.

Perhaps even more encouraging than Bowen’s attacking performance was his leadership. We know he’s an outstanding footballer, but being a captain requires something different. It requires the confidence to challenge teammates, demand better performances and take responsibility when things are going wrong.

And according to Veltman’s account, that’s exactly what Bowen did at half-time. Indeed, in his own post-match interview, the captain explained that he had urged his teammates not to hide or allow their shoulders to slump.

That is precisely the sort of leadership West Ham have been crying out for. I also have little doubt that working under Parker, and with Mark Noble around the club, could help Bowen develop further in that role. Both understand the importance of leadership, responsibility and the relationship between the players and supporters.

And if Bowen can combine those qualities with the extraordinary footballing ability he already possesses, West Ham will have one hell of a captain. He’s already demonstrated his importance as a player, but Wednesday night’s performance suggested he might be developing into the sort of leader who can inspire the entire team when things are going wrong.

There will quite rightly be plenty of analysis of last night’s remarkable comeback, particularly the tactical changes and the transformation in the team’s attitude. But it’s only right that Bowen receives the recognition he deserves, because he was absolutely brilliant.

And on a night when we can only hope West Ham finally began turning a corner after what has been a pretty miserable three years, our captain showed exactly why he remains the most important player at the football club.

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

With over a decade of professional sports media experience, he is a frequent West Ham United analyst and contributor for Sky Sports News, BBC Football Focus, and BBC Radio 5 Live. He previously served as an official video and content creator for West Ham United FC during the club's tenure at Upton Park and featured in the official documentary commemorating the historic final game at the Boleyn Ground.

A lifelong Hammer since the legendary 10-0 victory over Bury, when he isn't providing daily match analysis on the Hammers Chat YouTube Channel or broadcasting on X (@GONZObignose), he can be found walking his dog and restoring classic pinball machines.

Not only was a new Bowen unleashed playing like prime Paqueta assist mode in midfield but max Kilman looked unleashed as a fox in the box striker too. How far forward was he? Suddenly from first half no one in the box to second half every man and his dog busting a gut to get in on the action. Incredible turnaround.

‘It doesn’t have to be particularly complicated. Give Bowen the freedom to influence games and let the opposition worry about stopping him, rather than asking him to spend much of the match chasing possession in areas where he can’t do any damage.’

So true, Kris. Should always be the case that good players are allowed to play the game as they see it. No team should be limited by the coaching staff.

No doubt that Bowen is the best player in the West Ham squad and he does have days when he is difficult to stop, but he also has off days when he is very ordinary. As a captain, and in the context of Premier League football, he is not the ideal choice. I would hope that West Ham are able to bring in a strong defensive minded player with leadership qualities to relieve Bowen and let him get on with what he does best, rather than persisting with his development as a team captain. A little too much gushing praise for someone who only got a 4 rating last time out.

I thought he played more central in the 2nd half, and it paid off. He wasn’t as wide as he would normally find himself and I really think having him regularly on the ball made a difference.

I too thought it was a really positive and more influential performance from him – would love to see more of that!

#2101. Brian Madjo, 17, electrifies Villa despite Super Cup defeat by PSG

Unai Emery’s Aston Villa 2.0 remain under construction but from the wreckage of a difficult summer there has emerged a potential star for the future.

Emery may have now suffered four successive defeats in the Super Cup, yet the big positive from a balmy night in Salzburg was the performance of teenage forward Brian Madjo. Aged 17 years and 212 days, Madjo became the youngest player to start and score in this continental showpiece, just over a week after he was given permission to play for his club.

Signed from Metz for £10m in January, Madjo had been prevented from playing because of Fifa’s rules on the international transfer of minors. Villa’s appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport to have him registered was upheld on August 4 and what a prospect he appears.

Born in Enfield but raised in Luxembourg, there has been a huge buzz around him since his arrival in the new year.

Paris St-Germain have produced an abundance of talented teenagers over the years and Madjo did not look out of place here.Désiré Doué’s second-half strike secured PSG the Super Cup – contested by the winners of the Champions League and Europa League – for the second successive year, but Emery will have seen enough to give him renewed confidence.

Desire Doue puts PSG 2-1 ahead despite originally being flagged offside 🫣📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/vnMIZCWJaj

His team played with all the resilience and bravery that has become a trademark, epitomised by the powerful Madjo and another teenager in midfielder George Hemmings.

Emery said: “Brian has scored goals for us in pre-season and has shown his capacity to work in our idea. I am so happy because the young players were involved in our work and not playing last season.

“Of course there is still work to do but they showed they can play with us. They have responded fantastically and will then feel the confidence. With a loss you can never be happy but overall I am proud of all the players and everything we’ve done. Some changes will be needed but we’re confident.”

This was a fine Villa performance to silence the doom merchants who have been fearing a troubled season. After the painful sales of Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne, Villa are clearly a team in transition. They are operating under restrictions to comply with Uefa’s financial rules and there is still the possibility of another important player leaving before the transfer deadline day.

England centre-back Ezri Konsa remains a priority target for Premier League champions Arsenal, and was absent here. Konsa, Emiliano Martínez and Ollie Watkins were all granted extended leave after their participation in the World Cup, which has done little to ease the fears of supporters over more departures. The trio will return to training this weekend.

While some outsiders are predicting a difficult season for Villa, do not bother telling Emery. He has turned putting noses out of joint into an art form since sweeping into Villa Park and with him around anything feels possible.

The Basque remains optimistic about the future and those hopes will only have been underlined by the performance of Madjo. He bullied PSG centre-back Willian Pacho for much of the evening and even managed to steal the limelight from PSG’s magician Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

Hemmings, 19, has emerged from the academy and already made a real impression on his manager. Despite the high regard for those youngsters, this always appeared likely to be a tough proposition against a full-strength PSG team. Indeed, before this game in Salzburg only 39 per cent of Europa League winners have beaten their Champions League rivals in this fixture.

The French champions did start slowly, but had been cranking up the pressure before taking a 20th minute lead with a spectacular strike from their Georgian superstar.

Doué forced a save from Marco Bizot and, after Villa failed to clear, the loose ball landed in the path of Kvaratskhelia, who cut inside on the left to his right foot before smashing a shot into the roof of the net.

Khvicha Kvaratskhelia puts PSG 1-0 ahead vs Aston Villa 🔥📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/BIf8njpaSx

It was a strike of sheer power and accuracy, catching Bizot by surprise. PSG briefly appeared in control, but Villa responded superbly. In 17 minutes they created six goal-scoring chances before the outstanding Madjo finally made one of them count.

Before his goal, he had narrowly missed the target twice with a pair of headers from John McGinn’s crosses. Villa also had another opportunity 10 minutes before half-time, when Pacho’s mistake allowed Hemmings to run from the centre circle unopposed. As he entered the penalty area, the PSG defenders had raced back to recover and a promising moment ended with Madjo curling a shot wide.

Brian Madjo with a big chance to put Aston Villa level 😮📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/pqsC5Hor15

PSG goalkeeper Matvey Safonov then produced his first save just before the break, turning away Boubacar Kamara’s close-range header. Villa did carve out another golden chance when Madjo’s strength took hm past Pacho, but he hit the outside of the post. Madjo’s moment did come, though, as he once again bullied Pacho to divert a McGinn cross into the roof of the net.

Brian Madjo at 17-years-old scores in the UEFA Super Cup Final 🤯📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/PccX7FxjAr

Villa were buoyant, but it was PSG who scored the crucial second goal after Doué was awarded the goal following a VAR review. Doué was sent clear down the right by substitute Ousmane Dembélé and confidently beat Bizot, with reviews concluding that he had been played onside by Matty Cash.

The game was refereed by Omar Artan, the Somali referee who was supposed to officiate at the World Cup but was denied entry to the United States.

It became rather fractious as time began to tick away, with McGinn booked after complaining over the placement of a free-kick. Madjo was replaced by Tammy Abraham with 17 minutes left and this will be an evening he will never forget.

PSG (4-3-3): Safonov, Hakimi, Marquinhos, Pacho, Mendes (Hernandez 75), Neves (Ruiz 75), Vitinha, Emery, Akliouche, (Dembele 45), Doue (Mayulu 87), Kvaratskhelia (Buraldo 88).Substitutes: Chevalier (g), Zabarnyi, Digne, Fernandez, Barcola, Ndjantou, Mbaye.Villa (4-2-3-1): Bizot, Cash, Lindelof, Torres (Mings 80), Maatsen, Kamara (Bogarde 72), Gomes (Barkley 79), McGinn 7 (Alysson 73), Buendia, Hemmings, Madjo (Abraham 72).Substitutes: Wright (g), Asemota (g), Barkley, Nedeljkovic, Cisse, Rowe, Burrowes, Lynch.Booked: Gomes, Torres, McGinn.Referee: Omar Artan (Somalia).

After the officials and the Aston Villa players receive their medals, it is time for the 2026 Uefa Super Cup winners PSG to receive their medals. The last man up is their captain Marquinhos, who has won a staggering 40 trophies during his time at PSG. He takes the trophy from Uefa President Aleksander Ceferin and lifts it above his head alongside his teammates.

PSG are your 2026 UEFA Super Cup Champions 🏆📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/1qCKEQ0IPK

Both Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye have been heavily linked with moves to Liverpool this summer and neither player came off the bench for PSG tonight. Does that indicate that potentially those moves could be close, with neither played risked of picking up an injury?

Luis Enrique has now won 13 trophies with PSG. Serial winner 🏆 pic.twitter.com/RAsyI1Ui2s

💬 "We are ALWAYS hungry you know... we want more, we want more" Désiré Doué reflects on PSG's UEFA Super Cup Final win.📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/nwreU1Skz7

Aston Villa will take on Borussia Mönchengladbach on Saturday in their final game of pre-season before they take on Brighton on the south coast on the opening weekend of the new Premier League season.

PSG play Lens in the Trophée des Champions on Sunday before they kick off the defence of their Ligue 1 crown at home against Rennes.

Possession: PSG 61%- Aston Villa 39%Shots: 12-15Shots on target: 6-4Corners: 0-2Touches in opposition box: 29-34

Buendia has a late chance to equalise for Aston Villa from Maatsen’s cross but his header goes wide.

Not long after, the final whistle goes and PSG win the Super Cup for the second straight year. Last year they beat Tottenham on penalties, this time they beat Aston Villa 2-1. Unai Emery’s side acquitted themselves well and will regret some of their missed chances tonight. An entertaining affair in Salzburg.

PSG win back-to-back UEFA Super Cup's following goals from Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Desire Doue 🏆📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/vzMx6rGjuo

Dembele feeds a pass into the Villa box looking to pick out the run of Hakimi but there is slightly too much on it and Bizot is out to gather.

Into the final minute of added time we go.

Aston Villa are running out of time to find a late equaliser.

Maatsen brings Dembele down not far outside the Aston Villa box but play goes on as the latter gets up and shoots, with his effort saved by Bizot.

One final change for PSG as their other goalscorer tonight, Kvaratskhelia, is replaced by Beraldo. A defender comes on for an attacker as Luis Enrique’s side look to hold on for the victory.

Mayulu is coming on for Doue, whose goal may well have won back-to-back Super Cups for PSG.

The ball falls to Kvaratskhelia on the right side of the box and the Georgian chips it over Bizot but Cash is on hand to clear. Aston Villa then counter and Abraham feeds a pass forward at the perfect time to pick out the run of Alysson into the PSG box. Alysson then plays it across the six-yard box but neither Abraham nor Maatsen are there to meet the cross.

Double change for Aston Villa as Barkley and Mings replace Gomes and Torres, who were both on yellow cards.

Alysson, only just on the pitch, does brilliantly down Aston Villa’s right and drives into the PSG penalty area. His cross is parried away by Safonov straight into the path of Gomes, whose shot is blocked by Zaire-Emery.

PSG are making a double substitution as Ruiz and L Hernandez come on. Neves and Mendes, who had been struggling with cramp, go off.

Aston Villa are going to make a triple change as Abraham, Alysson and Bogarde come on. 17-year-old Madjo is one of those to be replaced as is McGinn, who has been booked as he goes off. The Aston Villa captain is distinctly unimpressed with the officials.

The space opens up for Mendes to take on the shot from range and he obliges, forcing Bizot into a decent save. Kvaratskhelia is unable to make contact with the follow-up. Mendes seems to be struggling with some cramp.

We are nearly 70 minutes into the game but Unai Emery has still not turned to his bench yet.

Aston Villa have an immediate chance to equalise through Hemmings but the 19-year-old’s effort from inside the box is straight at Safonov. That was a big chance for Hemmings.

Down the other end, Gomes is booked for a challenge from behind on Doue.

The VAR has checked it and there was no offside so the original decision is overturned and the goal is given. Doue is played in behind by Dembele down the right channel and is played onside by Cash on the far side. Doue takes it into the Villa penalty area and gets it onto his left foot. He curls it past Bizot and into the far corner.

Desire Doue puts PSG 2-1 ahead despite originally being flagged offside 🫣📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/vnMIZCWJaj

Doue has the ball in the Aston Villa net but the offside flag has gone up. However, has Cash played Doue onside?

Cash’s cross from the right picks out Buendia at the front post but the latter’s header is off target. Unai Emery will be pretty happy with his side’s performance through the hour mark.

Mendes is a touch fortunate not to be penalised for a foul on McGinn as the Aston Villa captain spun the Portuguese defender on halfway. The referee must have thought both players had a hold of each other but I would lean towards Mendes probably fouling McGinn.

Other than 10/15 minutes in and around Kvaratskhelia’s goal, Aston Villa have put in a good performance and have created more chances than PSG. If anything, it will be Villa who will be disappointed that they have not scored more than once.

Just inside the PSG penalty area, McGinn cuts onto his left to get his shot away and his deflected effort is saved by Safonov diving to his right.

One of Aston Villa’s coaches has been booked for some protestations after Torres is penalised for a foul on Doue. Torres is also booked for that challenge.

Two of Aston Villa’s best players tonight thus far have been teenagers; 19-year-old Hemmings and 17-year-old Madjo. Aston Villa have seen some key, senior players depart this summer but will take joy from the performances of this pair.

Luis Enrique has decided he needed to make a change at the break as Dembele replaces Akliouche, who was quiet on his official debut for PSG after his move from Monaco.

Incredible to think he is only 17 years and 212 days old. He’s been all over PSG centre-back Willian Pacho and thoroughly deserves his goal.

The teenager could even have had a hat-trick. What a second-half this could be.

Madjo has managed to steal the limelight from PSG’s Georgian magician Kvicha Kvaratskhelia, which is quite some achievement.

Possession: PSG 67%-33% Aston VillaShots: 6-10Shots on target: 2-2Corners: 0-2Touches in opposition box: 11-17

After one added minute, the first half is brought to an end and we are all square at 1-1 in Salzburg. Kvaratskhelia had put PSG in front but Madjo’s goal on the stroke of half-time has Aston Villa level at the break.

On the stroke of half-time, the 17-year-old levels for Aston Villa and finally takes his fourth big chance of the night. It is perhaps the hardest chance he has had as McGinn’s cross comes all the way to the back post. Madjo is being held by Pacho but somehow gets his foot to it and his shot goes into the roof of the net. What a moment for the 17-year-old!

Brian Madjo at 17-years-old scores in the UEFA Super Cup Final 🤯📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/PccX7FxjAr

Madjo has his third massive chance of this first half and this shot comes off the post. Buendia feeds a pass forward into the path of Madjo, who appeared to be blocked by Pacho but he outmuscles him. Madjo then fires towards goal but it strikes the outside of the post. In a parallel universe, Madjo could have ahd a first-half hat-trick.

Aston Villa have had a few great chances in this first half and there is another. A free-kick into the PSG penalty area causes issues for the French side and Kamara’s header towards goal is saved by Safonov.

Madjo has his second huge chance of this first half. Once more it is McGinn who provides the cross. The Scot does really well on the right side of the box to fake the cross with his left and instead delivers with his right. He picks out Madjo at the back post and the 17-year-old should score but his header misses the target. What a story it would have been had the 17-year-old scored two goals against the Champions League winners.

Aston Villa have just settled things down. Either side of Kvaratskhelia’s goal, they were on the ropes but have calmed things down.

Hemmings is played in and he could potentially have gone down twice under challenges from Hakimi and then Mendes. The ball then falls to 17-year-old Madjo on the left side of the box. He opens up his body and tries to curl into the far corner but his effort goes wide.

Referees are now hot on players taking too long over throw-ins, with Mendes falling foul of that. That is one of the fairly new rules that will be good for the game.

A huge chance for 17-year-old Madjo to equalise. McGinn picks out the young striker with a sublime cross from the right. Madjo is just eight yards out and has a free header but it goes just wide of the far post. Aston Villa should be level.

Brian Madjo with a big chance to put Aston Villa level 😮📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/pqsC5Hor15

After Aston Villa had made a solid start to this game, it is all PSG right now and Villa are on the ropes at the moment. PSG work it beautifully down their left after a sublime one-two between Mendes and Kvaratskhelia. Mendes drives down the left wing and has a cross into the box first-time which he declines. The Portuguese defender then has four different teammates that he could pick out in the penalty area but his cross misses all four.

PSG want a penalty. Kvaratskhelia shows great feet out on the left to drive into the Aston Villa penalty area. Gomes is on his back and Kvaratskhelia goes down. It did look like he was always looking to go down and it would have been very soft.

A few minutes after I said that Aston Villa had done a decent job of keeping PSG at bay, Luis Enrique’s side take the lead. Bizot had just made a great reflex save to deny Doue but he is unable to stop Kvaratskhelia’s effort. The Georgian cuts inside onto his right just inside the Aston Villa penalty area and gets his shot away quickly after quick feet. There is great venom on the shot and it beats Bizot, who thought Kvaratskhelia was going to go for the far corner but instead hit it at the near post. Could Bizot have saved that? Perhaps but Kvaratskhelia did belt that shot.

Khvicha Kvaratskhelia puts PSG 1-0 ahead vs Aston Villa 🔥📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/BIf8njpaSx

As you would expect, PSG are dominating possession but thus far have been unable to create any genuine chances, much to Aston Villa’s credit. But, with the players PSG have at their disposal, they can cause chaos in a moment.

Tensions just start to simmer. McGinn gives a foul away on Mendes, who then attempts to take the free-kick a good few yards further forward from where it was. McGinn repeatedly tries to stop Mendes from taking it further forward before the referee steps in to end the dispute.

Moments later, Kamara decides to shoot from range and his low, driving effort goes wide of Safonov’s right post. With Onana injured long-term and Tielemans now at Manchester United, Kamara’s importance to Aston Villa is even higher.

In last year’s Super Cup, PSG were stunned in the first hour against Tottenham as went 2-0 down before coming back to win on penalties. PSG have played fewer friendlies than Aston Villa up until this point so there may be a little more rustiness in Luis Enrique’s side than Unai Emery’s.

This is going to be a very tall order for Aston Villa, who look very different tonight to how they ended last season, up against a team of PSG’s calibre. Not only have Villa sold some key players like Rogers and Tielemans but the likes of Konsa and Watkins are yet to return after the World Cup.

McGinn is afforded too much space and time to cut onto his left foot out on the right and whip a dangerous cross towards the far post. Pacho is on hand to head away with a great defensive header.

Moments later, good work from Maatsen out on the left earns Aston Villa a corner. Unai Emery’s side have made a decent start to this game. Buendia’s delivery into the near post is headed away by Marquinhos.

We are under way in Salzburg, where it has been a very hot day but the temperature has cooled a touch with the sun having set in Austria.

Some huge banners are on display on the pitch, displaying not only the emblems of the two clubs but also images of the trophy lifts that have earned these sides a place in tonight’s game. Both sides emerge from the tunnel, past the trophies they won with the two captains carrying them out, and we are moments away from kick-off in Salzburg. Here is a reminder of how the sides line up tonight:

💬 " I am confident they're going to play today with the level we need" Unai Emery on the inclusion of João Gomes and Brian Madjo into Aston Villa's lineup. 📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/FCjBmGDcNo

Lucas Digne has only just swapped Aston Villa for PSG in recent days but he already comes up against his old teammates. He is on the bench for PSG tonight and could offer some good insight into Unai Emery’s side.

PSG forwards Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye have both been linked with moves to Liverpool this summer and both are on the bench for PSG tonight. As PSG close in on moves for Ferran Torres and Mika Godts, could Liverpool’s moves for Barcola and Mbaye accelerate in the next few days? Barcola has only recently returned to training after the World Cup and is joined on the bench by compatriot Ousmane Dembele. Maghnes Akliouche, who has joined PSG from Monaco this summer, starts tonight.

Brian Madjo is just 17-years-old but he starts up top for Aston Villa tonight against the Champions League winners, with Ollie Watkins yet to return after the World Cup.

“There is a lot of change but when you look at other clubs in England, there is a lot of change. What we have still is our main core, same manager, same methods and same desire to achieve more. A lot thought we reached our ceiling a few seasons ago and we proved them wrong. As long as we have that hunger to achieve more, Aston Villa fans can expect as much as possible.”

New Villa signing Alejandro Garnacho has been ruled out tonight as part of the concussion protocols.

Garnacho was signed from Chelsea last month and took a whack to his face in the recent game against BG Pathum in Thailand.

Team news is in 🔒 #PSGAVL pic.twitter.com/yeKkyIKiHQ

What will we learn from the “new Aston Villa” tonight? After the sales of Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne, this is a Villa team in transition.

Unai Emery virtually admitted last night it could be another slow start to the season, like last year. Villa face a full-strength PSG team hoping to win the Super Cup for the second time in a row.

I don’t think we can take much from this result tonight, whatever it is. Villa cannot be properly judged until the window closes. Don’t bother telling that to Unai Emery, though. He is ready to continue defying the doubters.

The Champions League and Europa League winners fight it out in the Uefa Super Cup in Salzburg as PSG take on Aston Villa. PSG took on English opposition in the Super Cup a year ago, when they played Tottenham. PSG fell 2-0 down in that game in Udine but scored two late goals to take it to penalties, where they won 4-3. These sides met in the Champions League knockout stages two seasons ago; PSG did progress from the quarter-final encounter as they went on to win the competition but not without a scare as Aston Villa did win at Villa Park and PSG only progressed 5-4 on aggregate. The two clubs have been involved in a transfer this week, with left-back Lucas Digne re-joining PSG from Aston Villa.

Aston Villa have played in the Super Cup once before back in 1982 when they took in Barcelona. They lost the first leg 1-0 over at Camp Nou but fought back to win the second leg 3-0 at Villa Park to claim the trophy. Aston Villa were last in action out in the Far East last Friday, falling to a 2-1 defeat to Bayern Munich in Hong Kong. It has been a big summer of change at the club, with key starters like Morgan Rogers and Youri Tielemans departing and the likes of Alejandro Garnacho and Joao Gomes arriving.

“I feel like the club is in a new era, with this possibility to fight for trophies,” Unai Emery told Uefa. “We are trying to be successful through, firstly, [building] a winning team, and then aiming for the positive consequences after it; winning trophies. To play the UEFA Super Cup is another opportunity to be there, the opportunity to win a trophy, to play against Paris Saint-Germain; the [best] team in the world now and another team we can compare [ourselves] with.”

Emery has confirmed that Ezri Konsa, Ollie Watkins and Emiliano Martinez will not be involved as they are still on their breaks following the World Cup.

PSG have now won back-to-back Champions Leagues, beating Arsenal in the final last season. They have only played a couple of friendlies in pre-season, losing 3-0 to Mallorca before drawing 1-1 against Manchester United. Luis Enrique’s side will take on Lens in the Trophée des Champions on Sunday before kicking off the defence of their Ligue 1 title at home to Rennes.

“I focus on renewing that desire to win again,” Enrique told Uefa. “It is difficult to keep winning. Right now, we have a unique challenge; something that is practically unprecedented in the history of European football, which is to draw level with Real Madrid if we can win a third consecutive Champions League. No-one in history has won three in a row, only Real Madrid. We can equal them. But I do not think there is any team in Europe more motivated than us.

“No-one rules out PSG any more. Two years ago, it was impossible to put us among the favourites; not impossible, but we were not one of the favourites. Now, no one would say that Paris Saint-Germain are not the favourites. That is something we have earned, but if we are going to maintain that position, we have to work even harder.”

PSG have added Monaco winger Maghnes Akliouche and Digne to their ranks this summer. They are also pushing to sign Ferran Torres from Barcelona and Mika Godts from Ajax. Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye have both been linked with moves to Liverpool but have been included in their squad for tonight’s game, as have Akliouche and Digne.

#2100. Assume just incompetence from this journalist on Newcastle United fans and not deliberate untruths

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

I read with interest these comments from a journalist about the Newcastle United fans.

I only saw the articles today (Thursday 5 November 2026).

It was published on Tuesday, the day after the 1-0 home defeat to Everton.

It was a lengthy article by The Telegraph billed as an ‘Exclusive’, the headline declaring ‘Newcastle players feel hamstrung by poor recruitment’…

The main thrust of the article was that The Telegraph claimed they had sources giving them an inside track regarding certain Newcastle United players, that they weren’t happy with the summer recruitment, nor happy with the tactics used by Matthias Jaissle.

The article was credited to both Matt Law and Luke Edwards of The Telegraph.

I have no idea whether or not this is what certain Newcastle United players have been saying. I am assuming this is the truth and the newspaper had one or more credible source(s) for this.

What I did find unacceptable though, was something else in the article. Well a couple of things.

This was when backing up the unhappiness of the players angle, when talking about the fans.

I am sure this was just incompetence from Luke Edwards, rather than intentional untruths.

Talking about the Everton match he stated:

‘For the first time in years, you could still get tickets for the game on matchday. Newcastle fans are drained and deflated. They are starting to wonder whether this team, playing such ugly and disjointed long-ball football, is still worthy of their passionate and unflinching support.

We have not heard a Newcastle team booed and whistled at St James’ Park since the bleak, dark days of the Steve Bruce era.’

The Everton match was exactly the same as normal. All of the normal (non-hospitality) tickets for Newcastle United fans were as usual sold out for this match to members when the ballot sale and queue sale happened. The match by match tickets split over these two routes as is always the case. This happened weeks before the match.

What DOES happen ahead of each home game is that season ticket holders can decide to try and sell their tickets via the club’s official ticketing site to members. This means that even on a matchday there will usually be some tickets available, whether due to illness or whatever reasons, including fans simply deciding they don’t want to go. It obviously varies how many game to game.

Here on The Mag we highlighted how late last season more than a thousand of these tickets were getting put up for resale for certain matches by season ticket holders, such as the Brighton one. Many of them getting bought and/or season ticket holders ending up still going to the match if nobody bought their ticket online.

There has actually been at least one match where there WERE in the past tickets still on sale by the club when it got to matchday AND they didn’t sell out. This was the Champions League home game against Qarabag on 24 February 2026 when the official attendance was 50,068 after United won the first leg 5-1 and the ticket prices had been raised to unreasonable levels.

The idea that until Monday night a Newcastle United team (and manager) had never been booed by the fans since the days of Steve Bruce is laughable.

I don’t believe in booing the Newcastle United team and/or manager, well not since Steve Bruce anyway….

However, it simply isn’t true that this hasn’t happened before Everton on Monday.

Indeed, if you go back to 28 February 2026, both the Newcastle United team and manager were booed at half-time and full-time against…Everton. Eddie Howe’s side trailing 2-1 at HT and 3-2 at the end.

That came during a period of five defeats in six home Premier League matches. There were certainly plenty of boos for instance in reaction to the 3-2 defeat to Brentford, the 2-1 loss to Bournemouth AND the 2-1 defeat to Sunderland.

There were other previous instances as well, certainly the 4-1 home defeat to Bournemouth I recall in a previous season.

There are a lot of negatives at the moment but best to stick to the facts.
